text.p: The Sound & Vision unit of Philips Electronics NV is on course to improve profits during 1997 as it cuts costs and develops new markets, its chief executive, Doug Dunn, said on Wednesday.

The arm, whose products range from televisions to interactive media systems, is part of the sprawling Consumer Products division of Philips which covers phones, domestic appliances and the loss-making German Grundig unit.
"I am not complacent. We made a significant positive cash contribution to Philips and we were profitable (in 1996)," Dunn said in a telephone interview.

"Were we hugely profitable? No. By this industry's standards (profits were) good. And we will improve on them this year. This year will be better than last. I'll say no more than that because to give away numbers would be inappropriate."

Sound & Vision accounts for over half the sales at the Philips Consumer Products division, which in 1996 turned over 24 billion guilders ($12.8 billion), making it by far the biggest contributor to group sales of 69.2 billion guilders.
Consumer Products, undergoing an extensive restructuring, delivered only a 10 million guilder operating profit in 1996, hammered by flagging markets and price erosion.
Stripping out the effects of restructuring, operating profit was 167 million guilders.

Dunn said the Sound & Vision unit, which began restructuring last year at the cost of an expected 6,000 jobs, had put in place new practices which meant cost savings through larger production centres and standardisation of components.

"I admit that we're making money by doing things more efficiently but also we're growing in units (sales) by 10 percent, we're also gaining market share in many areas," he said, pointing to market growth in portable audio in the U.S. market and a dominant European market position for large screen TV.
"Take the new growth areas in China and parts of Asia Pacific excluding Japan, we're growing at least in line with the market and in most countries ahead of the market," he said.

Further down the road, new digital technologies for use with the Internet and currently being readied for the market will open new markets around the world as entertainment and communication technologies continue to converge.

"Looking forward, there are the new products that will come along. There's absolute growth, not in new areas because it's the same consumer that will buy them, but it's in new types of products," Dunn said.

"The classical analogue mainstream products that you have at home will be with us for another eight years yet but in the process of that eight years we will see quite a movement in new areas based on digital technology, based on the web, based on digital satellite, digital cable, a whole range of new content and services coming into your home," he said.

These new products will respond to demand for interlinked communications and entertainment devices so that consumers can, for instance, bank from home or be contacted via a hand-held personal computer.
"Gradually you'll swap your existing black boxes and increasingly buy a system solution, a combination of boxes and features which will be Internet-connected," he said.

"There's about an eight- or 10-year overlap of traditional products and products with the new features. Right now you can buy from Philips a web box that connects your TV to the web -- so already that process has started."
Dunn said the new products would not have a huge financial impact for a few years but in the new millennium could prove a cornerstone for the division's revenues.

"They are of tremendous importance in positioning the brand...and in establishing the base for what will become very high sales in the year beginning 2000 and beyond," he added. ($ = 1.875 Dutch Guilders)
